CHIEF COMPLAINT
Second opinion regarding right index finger injury

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
50-year-old male presents for second opinion regarding right index finger sustained in motor vehicle accident in March 2026. Patient was a passenger in a vehicle that was rear-ended multiple times. He felt slung forward which caused his right index finger to stretch and go backward. He reports persistent pain and swelling since the injury, approximately three months ago. Patient cannot make a fist and describes pain as sometimes unbearable, with even driving causing discomfort. He is right-handed and works as an X-ray technician, requiring use of this hand for his occupation. He was previously seen by an orthopedist with referral to occupational therapy and had MRI imaging performed. Patient was offered a steroid injection but initially declined due to previous adverse reaction to dexamethasone (heart racing). He reports confusion regarding treatment recommendations, with conflicting information about whether injection would help or worsen the tear. Patient expresses frustration with medical care received and seeks second opinion regarding treatment options.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Denies diabetes and rheumatoid arthritis. Endorses persistent pain and swelling of right index finger. Endorses prior reaction to methylprednisolone causing itching and prior reaction to dexamethasone causing heart racing. On physical examination, endorses numbness in distal finger and sensation of tearing with attempted flexion.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
Denies diabetes
Denies rheumatoid arthritis

MEDICATIONS
Blood pressure medication

ALLERGIES
Dexamethasone - causes heart racing
Methylprednisolone - causes itching

FAMILY HISTORY
Not discussed.

SOCIAL HISTORY
Occupation: X-ray technician
Right-handed
Motor vehicle accident: passenger in rear-ended vehicle, March 2026

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
General: Pleasant, cooperative, healthy male, no distress
Cardiovascular: Heart rate regular rate and rhythm, 2+ radial pulse
Right hand/index finger: No swelling or bruising in palm over volar surface of index finger. Normal creases with slightly diminished creases over PIP of index finger compared to middle finger. Index finger rests in 10-degree PIP-flexed position. PIP joint tender to palpation. Distal aspect has area of numbness. Limited active flexion at DIP and PIP joints with sensation of tearing with movement attempts. Patient able to make fist. Extensor tendons intact. Collateral ligaments intact.

RESULTS
X-rays of right hand (four views): No bony abnormalities. Joint congruency throughout all lesser digits on right hand. No soft tissue shadows of concern. No arthritis.

MRI obtained 4/24/2026: Focal soft tissue swelling over right index MCP joint. Partial-thickness tear of right FDS (flexor digitorum superficialis) tendon. Fluid consistent with tenosynovitis around FDP and FDS tendons. Radial and ulnar collateral ligaments of index MCP joint intact. MCP joint capsule intact. Extensor tendons intact.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Post-traumatic severe stenosing tenosynovitis of right index finger with partial tear of flexor digitorum superficialis tendon. FDS is the less important of the two flexor tendons; FDP tendon is intact. Significant scar tissue and inflammation around FDS tendon is blocking excursion of other tendons.

Plan:
1. Steroid injection: Betamethasone 1 cc mixed with lidocaine 0.5 cc for flexor tendon sheath injection. First attempt resulted in dramatic and violent painful reaction to needle introduction with hand contortion and patient withdrawing hand with concern for secondary needle stick. Needle withdrawn. Patient counseled on importance of therapeutic steroid. Second attempt with same injection was performed. Scant blood from small palmar vein encountered, cleaned and band-aid applied. Patient reassured multiple times that no harm was done to finger.

2. Symptomatic management: Ice this evening. Ibuprofen as needed.

3. Physical therapy: Outpatient occupational therapy once weekly for 6 weeks with goal of full active and passive range of motion with no restrictions. Patient counseled that extensor tendons and collateral ligaments are intact, so no risk of tearing or breaking bone with aggressive movement. Splinting discouraged as it immobilizes rather than mobilizes.

4. Follow-up: Repeat injection may be needed. Safe to drive. Injection expected to improve pain over 3-5 days with continued improvement over next couple of weeks.
